summary: Teredo lets nodes behind one or more IPv4 NATs obtain IPv6 connectivity by tunneling IPv6 packets over UDP. It relies on Teredo servers and relays; the servers are stateless and handle only a small fraction of the traffic. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Teredo lets a host behind an IPv4 NAT exchange IPv6 packets by wrapping them in UDP packets. A server helps the host discover its public-facing address, while relays carry traffic to other IPv6 networks.

how does teredo work behind a nat
subtitle: How a host behind an IPv4 NAT can send IPv6 packets by carrying them inside UDP.

tldr.problem: A host behind an IPv4 Network Address Translator (NAT) may not be able to use ordinary IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling, because the NAT may not pass IPv4 packets with arbitrary payload types.
tldr.mechanism: Teredo carries IPv6 packets inside UDP. A client asks a stateless server to learn its externally mapped address and port, then uses bubbles to establish NAT mappings; relays forward traffic between Teredo and other IPv6 nodes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4380 presents Teredo as IPv6 access of last resort and defines an automatic sunset path when another form of IPv6 becomes available. It has been updated by RFC 5991, RFC 6081 and RFC 9601.

today: RFC 4380 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5991, RFC 6081 and RFC 9601. The RFC describes Teredo as an IPv6 service of last resort with a built-in sunset procedure.

sections.title: Why Teredo Tunnels IPv6 in UDP
sections.content:
Some IPv6 transition tunnels carry IPv6 directly inside IPv4. A NAT may not be configured to pass that payload, and a host behind the NAT cannot use a local IPv4 address as a globally reachable tunnel address. A tunnel broker can help, but may need to carry all traffic along an indirect route.

Teredo carries IPv6 packets as UDP payload because UDP is commonly passed through NATs. The system uses Teredo clients, stateless Teredo servers and IPv6 relays. Servers help with discovery and setup; relays route packets between Teredo clients and other IPv6 nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT may block IPv6 packets carried directly inside IPv4. Teredo puts each IPv6 packet inside UDP, which the RFC expects more NATs to pass.

sections.title: The Client, Server and Relay Roles
sections.content:
A client first qualifies with a server to learn whether its NAT allows Teredo and what IPv4 address and UDP port the outside world sees. It then builds a Teredo IPv6 address from the server's prefix and those mapped values. Servers are designed to remain stateless and avoid carrying ordinary data traffic.

A relay is an IPv6 router that advertises reachability for the Teredo prefix and forwards packets to Teredo clients. To reach a native IPv6 or 6to4 peer, the client discovers a suitable relay using an ICMPv6 echo request containing a random value; the reply helps the client learn the relay's IPv4 address and UDP port.
sections.plainLanguage: The server helps the client learn how to be reached through its NAT. A relay carries traffic between the Teredo network and other IPv6 networks.

sections.title: What a Teredo Address Contains
sections.content:
A Teredo IPv6 address contains the 32-bit service prefix, the server's IPv4 address, 16 flag bits, the client's mapped UDP port and the client's mapped IPv4 address. The global service prefix is 2001:0000::/32.

The mapped port and IPv4 address are obfuscated by inverting each bit: the port is XORed with 0xFFFF and the address with 0xFFFFFFFF. The cone flag records whether the client believes it is behind a cone NAT; the other specified flag bits are zero.
sections.plainLanguage: A Teredo address includes the server and the client's public-facing IPv4 address and UDP port. The client address and port are scrambled in the IPv6 address by inverting their bits.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Packet Size
sections.content:
In simple encapsulation, the IPv6 packet is the payload of a UDP datagram inside IPv4. When a server forwards some packets received from third parties, it may add an 8-octet origin indication that records the obfuscated source IPv4 address and UDP port.

Router Solicitation and Router Advertisement exchanges may also carry an authentication element with a client identifier, authentication value, nonce and confirmation byte. The default authentication algorithm uses HMAC with SHA1. The default link MTU should normally be the IPv6 minimum of 1280 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Most Teredo packets contain an IPv6 packet inside UDP and IPv4. A server can add an origin note, and setup messages can include data that helps authenticate the server.

sections.title: Qualification and NAT Mappings
sections.content:
During qualification, a client sends a Router Solicitation and waits for a Router Advertisement with an origin indication. The default timeout is 4 seconds and the maximum number of repetitions is 3. If the first exchange does not identify a cone NAT, the client tries the server's secondary IPv4 address; matching mapped address and port values indicate a restricted or port-restricted cone NAT, while different values indicate a symmetric NAT.

Clients behind non-cone NATs exchange Teredo bubbles, which are minimal IPv6 packets with no payload, to create mappings that allow return traffic. A client must not send a bubble less than 2 seconds after its previous bubble to that peer, or after 4 bubbles in 300 seconds without a direct response. Clients also refresh NAT mappings because those mappings expire.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks the server what address and port the NAT assigned. For some NAT types, small empty packets open a path so the other host's reply can get back through.

sections.title: Exposure, Spoofing and Sunset
sections.content:
Teredo makes a host reachable over IPv6, so a NAT's filtering no longer protects services listening on the Teredo address. The RFC recommends a local firewall and discusses IPsec as protection for IPv6 traffic. A nonce check helps detect a spoofed server response; a shared secret can provide stronger authentication.

The RFC calls Teredo an interim, last-resort transition mechanism. A client must stop acting as a Teredo client when it has IPv6 connectivity by another means. The document also describes brittleness from NAT classification, expiring mappings, extra relays and the need for bubbles.
sections.plainLanguage: A Teredo address can make a device reachable from the IPv6 Internet, so the device needs its own protection. The RFC expects Teredo clients to stop using the tunnel once another kind of IPv6 access is available.
